newsitem.title: USA: Republican lawmaker urges U.S. balanced budget.
newsitem.headline: Republican lawmaker urges U.S. balanced budget.

text.p: Freshman House Republican Kay Granger said on Saturday that Congress should make balancing the federal budget its first priority this year.

"Our first task must be to balance the federal budget. Balancing the budget will improve the quality of life for all Americans," Granger, a Texan, said in the Republican response to President Bill Clinton's weekly radio address.
"Our future financial security depends on balancing the budget. We must balance the budget now so that government can protect Social Security and Medicare in the future," she said.
Granger also urged passage of a constitutional amendment requiring a balanced budget every year.

She said a balanced budget amendment would force Congress and the federal government to examine all federal spending programs. "Congress will have to review the programs that are on the books and see where the money is accomplishing something, and where it is simply wasted.
"Those wasted dollars belong in your pockets, because you'll spend them better than Washington can," she added.
Granger was mayor of Fort Worth until she was elected to Congress last November.
Clinton has promised to work with the Republican-controlled Congress to balance the budget by the year 2002.

"Politically, historically and economically, the forces are in place to balance the budget," Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told the Senate Judiciary Committee on Friday, adding, "We are not far apart. Now we need to get the job done."
But Rubin said Clinton still opposed the balanced budget constitutional amendment.

"A balanced budget amendment is a threat to our economic health, will expose our economy to unacceptable risks and should not be adopted," Rubin said. "It would seriously increase the risk of default on national debt," he added.
It takes a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate to pass a constitutional amendment and to send it to the states for ratification.

The House passed a balanced budget amendment in 1995 but it failed by one vote in the Senate. Republican leaders have pledged to try again to pass the amendment early this year but its chances are uncertain because House Republicans lost nine seats last November. Senate Republicans gained two seats.
